doc.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: Kenny Davern and the bass saxophone
title: Written bass parts and the move from two-beat to four-beat
summary: Wind bass parts are written out to avoid clashes with piano; he discusses how the string bass helped jazz shift to four-beat.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: With the music on most of the arrangements that you play, are all the bass parts written out?

Yeah. For the wind basses, for the tuba and the bass saxophone. For the string bass part, when it’s more of a free thing for swing, we’ll have chord changes in there. When you’re talking with the wind bass, either the tuba or the bass sax, he’s usually doubling the piano, and that reinforces, so you really want to have a precise bass part so that you don’t have these clashes. Like I’ll play the root and he’ll play the fifth, or he’ll play the fifth and I’ll play the root. It gets a little muddy down there you know. When you’ve got higher instruments it’s not that bad to have a little flavor of that sort. But you really want to lock it in with the same bass notes.
Do you think that — this is an awful general question — when music moved from sort of two-beat into four-beat, how much was the string bass a role in that?

Well you know I hear people phrasing in four, at least the horn, even with the two-beat feel going on. But I think when the musicians eventually got the idea and the feel of the pulsing four-beat they really didn’t want to go back. And so the tuba can do that and in the early days of like John Kirby where he did play some four-beat on the tuba, it was too unwieldy. And so once the string bass got ahold of that sound, and it was time for a change. You know jazz is always evolving, and putting the banjo away and getting the guitar with a kind of a softer feel, you know it just was one of those progressions. And musicians were always looking for something new and to claim their own development in jazz I think.
